item.title: A/B testing, through the Bayesian lens
item.description: The frequentist reading of the ramen test assumes both recipes are identical and asks how often luck alone would produce a gap that big, in Neal Patel's worked example. item.title: MCMC samples the posterior you cannot calculate
item.description: When a Bayesian posterior is too tangled to calculate directly, Markov Chain Monte Carlo learns it by sampling instead of solving it: a chain wanders through possible parameter values and spends more time where the posterior is high, so the values it visits build up a picture of the full distribution. In a sports-betting model for a team's true win probability, that might mean 10,000 samples…
item.content:encoded: When a Bayesian posterior is too tangled to calculate directly, Markov Chain Monte Carlo learns it by sampling instead of solving it: a chain wanders through possible parameter values and spends more time where the posterior is high, so the values it visits build up a picture of the full distribution. In a sports-betting model for a team's true win probability, that might mean 10,000 samples centered near 0.58 with 90% of them between 0.51 and 0.65, a best guess with honest uncertainty for judging an edge, but only if the chain has mixed well and converged.

item.title: Big Idea: The Doomsday Argument — Daily Learning
item.description: You are roughly the 117 billionth human ever born, by the Population Reference Bureau's estimate updated in January 2026, and the Doomsday Argument, first proposed by astrophysicist Brandon Carter in 1983, applies the Copernican principle to that rank: if you were equally likely to be any human who will ever live, landing this early favors totals of a few hundred billion over trillions still to…
item.content:encoded: You are roughly the 117 billionth human ever born, by the Population Reference Bureau's estimate updated in January 2026, and the Doomsday Argument, first proposed by astrophysicist Brandon Carter in 1983, applies the Copernican principle to that rank: if you were equally likely to be any human who will ever live, landing this early favors totals of a few hundred billion over trillions still to come, because Bayesian updating penalizes the huge totals that would make your position a freak coincidence. It predicts no extinction date, and critics question whether birth rank is truly random, who counts in the reference class, and whether the sampling assumption holds at all, so what, if anything, should your mere position in history tell you about humanity's future?

Searle's point was that a computer does the same, shuffling symbols by syntax without grasping semantics, which leaves today's fluent AI with his question: if you can't tell the difference…

item.title: A credible interval says what you think 95% means
item.description: Writing in June 2014, Jake VanderPlas explained that a 95% confidence interval is about the procedure: repeat it many times and about 95% of such intervals would capture the truth, while this one interval either contains it or does not. A 95% credible interval makes the direct claim most people intend, that given the data and the prior there is a 95% probability the truth lies inside, so a poker…
item.content:encoded: Writing in June 2014, Jake VanderPlas explained that a 95% confidence interval is about the procedure: repeat it many times and about 95% of such intervals would capture the truth, while this one interval either contains it or does not. A 95% credible interval makes the direct claim most people intend, that given the data and the prior there is a 95% probability the truth lies inside, so a poker tracker reporting a win rate of 5 big blinds per 100 hands with a credible interval of 1 to 9 really does mean a 95% chance the player's real edge is in 1 to 9.

item.title: Maxwell's Demon Sorts Molecules by Speed
item.description: In 1867, James Clerk Maxwell imagined a tiny being who opens a trapdoor in a divided box only for fast molecules one way and slow molecules the other, making one side hotter and the other colder without apparent work and seemingly violating the second law of thermodynamics, which says entropy shouldn't decrease on its own. The century-long puzzle resolves in the demon's memory: it must record and…
item.content:encoded: In 1867, James Clerk Maxwell imagined a tiny being who opens a trapdoor in a divided box only for fast molecules one way and slow molecules the other, making one side hotter and the other colder without apparent work and seemingly violating the second law of thermodynamics, which says entropy shouldn't decrease on its own. The century-long puzzle resolves in the demon's memory: it must record and eventually erase what it sees, and erasing information costs energy and produces entropy, showing information itself is physical and raising what that cost means for knowledge, prediction, and any mind, human or machine, trying to outsmart randomness.

item.title: Testing 20 ideas lifts false alarms to 64%
item.description: Test one hypothesis at the usual 5% level and you accept a 1-in-20 chance of a false alarm when nothing is really there. Test 20 independent ideas at once (20 player props, 20 poker tendencies, 20 features in a dataset), and the chance that at least one looks significant by pure luck jumps to about 64%, not 5%. That is why p-hacking happens: keep slicing the same data enough ways and something…
item.content:encoded: Test one hypothesis at the usual 5% level and you accept a 1-in-20 chance of a false alarm when nothing is really there. Test 20 independent ideas at once (20 player props, 20 poker tendencies, 20 features in a dataset), and the chance that at least one looks significant by pure luck jumps to about 64%, not 5%. That is why p-hacking happens: keep slicing the same data enough ways and something will inevitably light up. The fix is to adjust for how many looks you took, for example with a Bonferroni correction, or to pre-register what you actually plan to test before you start.

item.title: Word of the Day: inchoate — Daily Learning
item.description: Inchoate (in-KOH-it) is an adjective for something just begun and not yet fully formed or developed, rudimentary and imperfectly shaped. item.content:encoded:
stochastic — stuh-KAS-tik
Part of speech: adjective
Definition: Randomly determined; describing a process or system that involves chance or probability, so its future states can be described with distributions rather than a single certain outcome.
Example: "A weather forecast is stochastic at heart — it doesn't promise rain at 3 p.m., it gives you a 70% chance and lets you plan around the uncertainty."

item.title: Cleveland-Cliffs stock jumps 14% on 2027 outlook
item.description: Cleveland-Cliffs expects 2027 adjusted EBITDA to exceed $4 billion, based on new contracts it has already signed. Tariffs at 50% on raw steel are pushing up domestic prices, CEO Lourenco Goncalves said.

item.content:encoded: Cleveland beat Baltimore 13-10 on Andre Szmyt's 37-yard field goal as time expired, and Pittsburgh's overtime win later left the Browns, Ravens and Steelers all 4-2 atop the AFC North. The rest of Sunday, in brief: the new AP poll put Miami first, BYU second and Ohio State third after the Buckeyes' win at Indiana; the Big 12 admitted BYU's 28-24 win over Notre Dame on Saturday ended a second early; Sunday's other finals included Texans 34, Jaguars 31, Bears 31, Falcons 23, Titans 26, Colts 20, Patriots 26, Jets 19, Saints 34, Giants 27, Panthers 25, Eagles 14, Steelers 26, Buccaneers 19 in overtime, Cardinals 18, Rams 16, Chiefs 22, Chargers 6 and Bills 33, Raiders 30; tonight brings Cowboys at Packers at 8:20 ET on NBC and Peacock with Green Bay favored by 1.5; tomorrow brings Commanders at 49ers with San Francisco favored by 7.5 and chasing a record 56th Monday Night Football win; Anthropic announced it will commit 5% of its shares to a public benefit fund; futures edged up Sunday night after the S and P 500 fell 1.9% and the Nasdaq fell 4.5% last week in a sell-off concentrated in chip names; the earnings week ahead features SpaceX on Tuesday and Tesla and Meta on Wednesday; Reuters reported a Ukrainian attack of more than 1,000 drones on the St Petersburg oil terminal that killed one person and injured 15; the Festival in a Box: Atlanta 2026 sale, announced on October 5, opens tomorrow at 10 in the morning Mountain Time at $249.99 with a limit of two per customer; and researchers reported in Physical Review Letters a new quantum state called a fractional Fermi sea, created with ultracold cesium atoms in a one-dimensional system.
